title: China Launches 24th Batch of Guowang Internet Satellites Days After Rocket Failure
excerpt: A Long March 12 rocket deployed nine satellites for China's broadband megaconstellation from Hainan, resuming launches just six days after a Long March 7A exploded over the South China Sea.
body:
• China launched the 24th batch of nine satellites for its Guowang broadband megaconstellation on August 16 using a Long March 12 rocket from Hainan
  • The launch came just six days after a Long March 7A rocket suffered a catastrophic structural failure during launch, destroying a communications satellite
  • China's Guowang constellation now has over 170 satellites in low Earth orbit, competing with SpaceX's Starlink and Shanghai's Qianfan constellation
  • A Chang'e 7 lunar south pole mission is expected to launch from the same spaceport complex as early as August 24

China successfully deployed the 24th batch of satellites for its Guowang broadband internet megaconstellation on August 16, using a Long March 12 rocket launched from the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site. The mission placed nine communication satellites into low Earth orbit, according to the China Satellite Network Group.

Quick Recovery After Failure

The successful launch came just six days after a Long March 7A rocket suffered a catastrophic failure approximately 80 seconds after liftoff from the nearby Wenchang Space Launch Site on August 10. The rocket experienced what observers described as a structural breakup between its second and third stages near the point of maximum aerodynamic pressure, according to NASASpaceFlight. The vehicle's flight termination system was activated, destroying the rocket and its payload — the ChinaSat-4B communications satellite — with debris falling into the South China Sea.

"This is the vehicle's second failure in eighteen missions."

— NASASpaceFlight report on Long March 7A

The rapid turnaround demonstrated China's ability to compartmentalize launch failures and maintain pace on its constellation deployment schedule. The Long March 12 that carried the Guowang batch is a different rocket family from the failed Long March 7A, operating from the adjacent commercial launch facility.

The Guowang Constellation Race

With this latest batch, China's Guowang constellation has surpassed 170 satellites in orbit, part of a planned network of more than 10,000 satellites designed to provide global broadband internet coverage. The project is operated by China SatNet, a state-owned enterprise established specifically to manage the constellation.

Guowang is one of two major Chinese satellite internet constellations under construction. The other, Qianfan (also known as Spacesail), is backed by the Shanghai municipal government and reached 200 satellites in orbit following launches in June, according to SpaceNews. Qianfan plans to deploy more than 15,000 satellites, with the first phase comprising 1,296 spacecraft.

Together, the two Chinese constellations aim to rival SpaceX's Starlink, which currently operates more than 6,000 satellites and has become the dominant global provider of satellite internet. India's own plans for a satellite broadband network remain in earlier stages of development.

Busy Period for Chinese Space Program

The Long March 12 launch was the seventh flight for the rocket type, which has become a workhorse for Guowang deployments since its maiden flight in November 2024. Each mission carries nine satellites to their target orbit at approximately 1,156 kilometers altitude.

China has conducted over 53 orbital launches in 2026 so far, deploying satellites across communications, Earth observation, and AI-powered computing applications. The Hainan spaceport complex is also preparing for the launch of the Chang'e 7 lunar mission, which will explore the Moon's south pole near Shackleton crater. That mission's launch window opens on August 24, with a Chang Zheng 5 rocket already at the launch facility.

Implications for Global Connectivity

For the Indian tech community and diaspora, China's accelerating satellite internet program represents both competition and a shifting landscape in global connectivity. As India's own satellite broadband ambitions take shape, the pace of Chinese deployment — now averaging roughly one Guowang batch launch per month — sets a benchmark that other space programs are measuring themselves against.
